newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australia unveils law to end Aboriginal land row.
newsitem.headline: Australia unveils law to end Aboriginal land row.

text.p: The Australian government on Friday unveiled a draft law aimed at ending a divisive land rights row between farmers and Aborigines that has threatened the country's valuable rural industries.

A senior MP said the government hoped to pass the legislation, guaranteeing farmers rights to land they have leased since European settlement and allowing Aborigines limited access for traditional purposes, by the end of the year.
"I think all parties should have the objective of seeking to have it through by the end of the year," the prime minister's parliamentary secretary, Nick Minchin, told reporters.

Minchin said the government of Prime Minister John Howard would continue to consult interest groups and the opposition Labor party, but would not accept any substantial change to the thrust of its plan.
"The prime minister has made it quite clear that the government's position is that the ... plan itself ... is not negotiable, but the legislation to give effect to it is," he said.
Aboriginal groups say the legislation aims to meet the concerns of rich farmers and miners at the expense of indigenous people who have only just won rights over ancestral lands.

Native title laws were introduced by the former Labor government three years ago, but became a vital political issue when the High Court decided last December that land leased to farmers could be liable to Aboriginal claim.
The court did not specify those native land rights, creating confusion about land title that farmers and miners said was hitting their business and future investment plans.
The government has threatened an early election if Labor and other non-government parties sought to derail the plan in parliament.
